hints: Notice the two key observations in the stem: most $\alpha$-particles go straight through, but a very small proportion rebound through more than $90^{\circ}$.
Link the bending and rebounding of positive $\alpha$-particles to electrostatic repulsion from a tiny, massive, positively charged centre.
Ask yourself which observation would tell you the nucleus is split into protons plus uncharged neutrons, rather than just being one charged mass.
walkthrough: Identify the evidence: most $\alpha$-particles are undeflected, some are deflected by a small angle, and very few rebound back toward the source.
Most passing straight through means the atom is mainly empty space where the $\alpha$-particle meets no significant mass or charge.
Deflection and especially rebound of positively charged $\alpha$-particles requires repulsion by a concentrated positive charge, so the nucleus is charged.
Rebound through more than $90^{\circ}$ also requires the $\alpha$-particle to hit something much heavier than itself in a tiny volume, so most atomic mass is in the nucleus.
Nothing in the angles or counting rates distinguishes different particles inside that centre, so proton-neutron composition needs later evidence. This is option C.

options.A: This can be concluded because most $\alpha$-particles pass straight through the foil with no deflection, showing they meet nothing in most of the atomic volume.
options.B: This can be concluded because rebound through more than $90^{\circ}$ requires a head-on collision with a centre much more massive than the $\alpha$-particle.
options.C: This cannot be concluded from scattering angles alone because the experiment only shows a small, massive, charged centre and gives no evidence about separate protons and neutrons inside it.
options.D: This can be concluded because deflection and repulsion of the positively charged $\alpha$-particles must be due to electrostatic repulsion from a concentrated positive charge.
